title: What are Flink SQL catalogs (HiveCatalog, JdbcCatalog, in-memory default catalog), how do they store table metadata persistently, and why are they important for production (table definitions survive job restarts, shared across teams)?
shortTitle: What are Flink SQL catalogs and why are they important for production

s1_definition.profdef: A Flink SQL catalog is the metadata store that holds the definitions of databases, tables, views, and functions that Flink SQL can query. The default in-memory catalog, called the GenericInMemoryCatalog, keeps these definitions only in the running session's memory, so they vanish when the job or SQL client stops. A HiveCatalog persists metadata in a Hive Metastore, which is a shared relational store, so table definitions survive restarts and are visible to every job and team that connects to the same metastore. A JdbcCatalog connects to an external relational database such as PostgreSQL and exposes its real tables as Flink tables automatically, so you do not have to redeclare them. Catalogs are what make table definitions durable, reusable, and centrally governed in production.
s1_definition.analogy: When the National Bank of India writes SQL against its transaction streams, every table like accounts or transactions needs a definition that says where the data lives and what columns it has. The default in-memory catalog is like writing those definitions on a whiteboard: the moment the room is cleared, they are gone, and the next person has to write them all again. A HiveCatalog is like storing those definitions in a shared central register that every department can read, so the accounts table defined by the payments team is instantly usable by the fraud team, and it is still there after the server reboots overnight.
s1_definition.oneliner: A Flink SQL catalog is the metadata store for tables and functions; the in-memory one forgets on restart, while HiveCatalog and JdbcCatalog persist and share definitions across jobs and teams.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Flink SQL catalog is the metadata store that holds the definitions of databases, tables, views, and functions that Flink SQL can query. The default in-memory catalog, called the GenericInMemoryCatalog, keeps these definitions only in the running session's memory, so they vanish when the job or SQL client stops. A HiveCatalog persists metadata in a Hive Metastore, which is a shared relational store, so table definitions survive restarts and are visible to every job and team that connects to the same metastore. A JdbcCatalog connects to an external relational database such as PostgreSQL and exposes its real tables as Flink tables automatically, so you do not have to redeclare them. Catalogs are what make table definitions durable, reusable, and centrally governed in production.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When the National Bank of India writes SQL against its transaction streams, every table like accounts or transactions needs a definition that says where the data lives and what columns it has. The default in-memory catalog is like writing those definitions on a whiteboard: the moment the room is cleared, they are gone, and the next person has to write them all again. A HiveCatalog is like storing those definitions in a shared central register that every department can read, so the accounts table defined by the payments team is instantly usable by the fraud team, and it is still there after the server reboots overnight.

**One line to remember:** A Flink SQL catalog is the metadata store for tables and functions; the in-memory one forgets on restart, while HiveCatalog and JdbcCatalog persist and share definitions across jobs and teams.

sections.s2_technical:
Flink SQL organises metadata in a three-level namespace: catalog, then database, then object such as a table or view. When you write `SELECT * FROM accounts`, Flink resolves it against the current catalog and database, or you can fully qualify it as `catalogName.databaseName.accounts`. The catalog is the top-level container, and Flink lets you register several catalogs in one session and switch between them with `USE CATALOG hive_catalog`.

The default catalog is the GenericInMemoryCatalog. Every CREATE TABLE you run lives only in the heap of the current TableEnvironment. This is fine for quick experiments, but when the SQL client exits or the job restarts, all definitions are lost, so you must re-run every DDL. That is unacceptable in production where dozens of jobs share the same tables. The HiveCatalog solves this by storing Flink's table metadata in a Hive Metastore, which is backed by a relational database such as MySQL. You register it with `CREATE CATALOG hive_catalog WITH ('type' = 'hive', 'hive-conf-dir' = '/opt/hive-conf')`. Now a table you create is written into the metastore and is durable: restart the cluster, reconnect, and the table is still there. It is also shared, so one team defines the accounts table once and every other team uses it without redeclaring the connector options. The HiveCatalog can even expose existing Hive tables directly for batch queries.

The JdbcCatalog is different in spirit. You point it at a live relational database with `CREATE CATALOG pg_catalog WITH ('type' = 'jdbc', 'base-url' = 'jdbc:postgresql://host:5432/', 'default-database' = 'bank', 'username' = '...', 'password' = '...')`, and it automatically surfaces that database's real tables as Flink tables, mapping their columns and types, so you can query them without writing any CREATE TABLE at all. The senior nuances are these. First, catalogs separate the where-is-the-data concern from the query logic, which is central to governance: access control, lineage, and discovery all hinge on a persistent catalog. Second, in production you almost never rely on the in-memory catalog for shared tables; you use a HiveCatalog or an enterprise catalog so definitions are a managed asset, often created by data engineering and consumed by many jobs. Third, catalogs also store functions and views, so a reusable business function such as a currency converter is defined once and shared. Fourth, modern deployments increasingly back the catalog with a lakehouse metastore such as the Iceberg or Paimon catalog for full table-format integration. Understanding that the catalog is the backbone of metadata durability and sharing, not just a convenience, is what distinguishes someone who has operated Flink SQL at team scale.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India several teams write Flink SQL against the same core tables such as accounts and transactions, and when each team redefined those tables in its own in-memory session, the definitions drifted, broke on restart, and had to be re-entered after every deployment. This is exactly why a persistent, shared catalog matters: one durable definition that survives restarts and is visible to all jobs.

Problem 2 — When a job restarted after a nightly patch, every in-memory table definition was gone and the job failed until someone re-ran all the DDL by hand. This is exactly the restart-survival property that a HiveCatalog provides, because the metadata lives in an external metastore rather than in the job's heap.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that models how a catalog stores and resolves table metadata, and the difference between an in-memory catalog and a persistent one. We define a `TableDefinition` holding a table name and its connector options, a `Catalog` interface with register, lookup, and listing, an `InMemoryCatalog` that loses everything when a new instance is created to mimic a restart, and a `PersistentCatalog` that writes definitions to a backing store that survives a simulated restart. A `CatalogDemo` main class registers the accounts and transactions tables, simulates a restart of each catalog, and prints which definitions survived, so the production benefit is obvious.

The catalog DDLs the demo models:

```sql
-- catalogs.sql
-- Persistent, shared metadata via Hive Metastore
CREATE CATALOG hive_catalog WITH (
    'type'          = 'hive',
    'hive-conf-dir' = '/opt/hive-conf'
);

-- Auto-expose a live PostgreSQL database's tables
CREATE CATALOG pg_catalog WITH (
    'type'             = 'jdbc',
    'base-url'         = 'jdbc:postgresql://db.bank.internal:5432/',
    'default-database' = 'bank',
    'username'         = 'flink_ro',
    'password'         = '${DB_PASSWORD}'
);

USE CATALOG hive_catalog;
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id STRING, holder_name STRING, balance DECIMAL(15,2),
    PRIMARY KEY (account_id) NOT ENFORCED
) WITH ('connector'='kafka','topic'='accounts','format'='debezium-json');
```

# Run the demo
java -cp target/flink-catalog-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.flink.cat.CatalogDemo

sections.s5_journey:
The input is two table definitions, accounts and transactions, and two catalogs, one in-memory and one persistent, each of which is restarted to simulate a nightly patch.

Step 1. The accounts and transactions definitions are registered in the in-memory catalog. They live in that instance's heap. Listing the catalog shows both tables.

Step 2. The in-memory catalog is restarted, which creates a fresh empty instance, exactly as a job restart gives a fresh heap. Listing the restarted catalog shows an empty list, because the definitions were never persisted anywhere. This is the production pain: every restart loses the metadata and someone must re-run all DDL.

Step 3. The same two definitions are registered in the persistent catalog, which writes them to a shared metastore store that lives outside the catalog instance. Listing shows both tables.

Step 4. The persistent catalog is restarted, which reconnects to the same shared metastore rather than creating a fresh store. Listing the restarted catalog still shows both tables, because the metadata survived in the metastore. A different team, represented by the fraud-team lookup, can immediately resolve the accounts definition without redeclaring it. This is exactly the restart-survival and sharing benefit that HiveCatalog gives in production.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Flink SQL catalog is the metadata store that holds the definitions of databases, tables, views, and functions that the SQL engine can see, organised as a three-level namespace of catalog, then database, then object. The default catalog is the GenericInMemoryCatalog, which keeps every definition only in the running session's heap, so the moment the SQL client exits or the job restarts, all those definitions are gone and you have to re-run every CREATE TABLE. That is fine for experiments but a serious problem in production, where many jobs depend on the same tables.

The persistent catalogs fix this. A HiveCatalog stores Flink's table metadata in a Hive Metastore backed by a relational database, so the definitions are durable, they survive cluster and job restarts, and they are shared, meaning one team defines the accounts table once and every other team queries it without redeclaring the connector options. A JdbcCatalog works differently: you point it at a live relational database and it automatically exposes that database's real tables as Flink tables, mapping columns and types, so you do not write any DDL at all for those tables. The senior points I stress are that the catalog is the backbone of governance, because access control, lineage, and discovery all depend on persistent metadata, that production deployments almost never use the in-memory catalog for shared assets, and that modern lakehouse setups back the catalog with an Iceberg or Paimon catalog for full table-format integration.

At the National Bank of India several teams, payments, fraud, and reporting, all wrote Flink SQL against the same core tables such as accounts and transactions. Early on each team redefined those tables in its own in-memory session, so the definitions drifted, and every nightly restart wiped them out, forcing someone to re-enter all the DDL by hand before jobs would run again. We moved the metadata into a HiveCatalog backed by a shared metastore, and that single change gave us two concrete wins: the definitions survived every restart because they lived outside the job's heap, and the fraud team could immediately query the accounts table that the payments team had defined, with no duplication and no drift. Being able to explain why the in-memory catalog loses metadata on restart, how HiveCatalog and JdbcCatalog make it durable and shared, and why that durability is the foundation of metadata governance is exactly what shows I have run Flink SQL at team scale rather than just in a single notebook.
